MUQATIL:12:41-42/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:41-42/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:41-42/r1.claim: Joseph predicts that the cupbearer will leave prison in three days, return to his work, and serve his master wine; the baker will be executed and eaten by birds.

MUQATIL:12:41-42/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:41-42/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:41-42/r2.claim: When the baker tried to deny the dream, Joseph said the outcome was settled whether or not they had truly dreamed it.

TAB-FULL:v13p167/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p167/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p167/r1.claim: The one who serves his master wine is the dreamer who saw himself pressing wine; the other, whose bread birds eat, will be crucified and birds will eat from his head.

TAB-FULL:v13p167/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p167/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p167/r2.claim: Rabb here means master or king; qadiya al-amr means the matter being asked about is finished and God's decree upon them has taken effect.

TAB-FULL:v13p167/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p167/r3.speaker: عبد الله
TAB-FULL:v13p167/r3.claim: Ibn Masud reports that the two youths denied having seen dreams after Yusuf interpreted them, but Yusuf said the matter was already decided.

TAB-FULL:v13p169/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p169/r1.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v13p169/r1.claim: Ibn Ishaq identifies Mujlith as the one crucified and Nabu as the one restored to his former service and accepted by his master.

TAB-FULL:v13p169/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p169/r2.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v13p169/r2.claim: Mujahid says the prediction had taken effect exactly as Yusuf interpreted when the youths claimed they had only been playing.

TAB-FULL:v13p169/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p169/r3.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB-FULL:v13p169/r3.claim: Ibn Jurayj quotes the phrase 'in which you seek a decision' without adding a further gloss.

ZAJJAJ:v3p110/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p110/r4.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p110/r4.claim: The cupbearer is the one who will serve wine to his master, the king. Sāqā means to hand someone a drink, while asqā means to provide water or irrigation.

ZAJJAJ:v3p111/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p111/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p111/r1.claim: When the condemned man denied having seen a dream, Joseph told him the predicted crucifixion would still happen, just as he knew what food would arrive.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r1.claim: Joseph told Majlath he would be crucified and birds would eat from his head, while Nabū would return to his post and regain his master's favor.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r2.speaker: ابن جريج
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r2.claim: A report attributed to Muhammad ibn Abbas says Joseph delayed interpretation because it foretold execution; the royal meal was sent to a prisoner intended for death, and Joseph first spoke of food to prompt their repeated request.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r3.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r3.claim: The prisoners panicked at the interpretations and said they had seen nothing; Joseph replied that the matter they asked about had been decided.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r4.claim: When the prisoners said they had seen nothing, Joseph's “the matter is decided” meant that the interpretation had occurred.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r5.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2147/r5.claim: The two prisoners had lied to test Joseph; after his interpretation they said they had only been playing, but he said the decision was already made.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2148/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2148/r1.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2148/r1.claim: Joseph says the matter they had asked about was inevitable.

NAHHAS:v2p329/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p329/r3.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p329/r3.claim: Most linguists distinguish giving a drink from providing water; the Qur'anic form supports the latter despite a poem claiming synonymy.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p335/r1.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p335/r1.speaker: author
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p335/r1.claim: The referenced form may be a plural of عشوة, meaning darkness, with its separate portions motivating the plural.

IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r5.author: Ibn Jinnī
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r5.speaker: عكرمة والجحدري
IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p343/r5.claim: ʿIkrimah and al-Jaḥdarī read فيسقى ربه خمرا, making the cupbearer's good outcome parallel to the other prisoner's punishment.

THALABI:v5p224/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p224/r1.speaker: ابن مسعود
THALABI:v5p224/r1.claim: Ibn Masʿud says the two prisoners admitted they had seen nothing and were only testing Joseph; Joseph replied that the matter had already been decreed.

THALABI:v5p224/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p224/r2.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي
THALABI:v5p224/r2.claim: Abu Ruzayn transmits the Prophet’s saying that a dream remains suspended until interpreted, is one forty-sixth of prophecy, and should be shared only with a person of judgment.

THALABI:v5p224/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p224/r3.speaker: أنس
THALABI:v5p224/r3.claim: Anas transmits a prophetic report that a dream is realized according to its first interpreter.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r1.claim: The cupbearer, whose dream concerned pressing grapes, will survive and resume serving wine to his master.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r2.claim: The baker, whose dream showed birds eating from bread on his head, will be killed by crucifixion; he was the king's baker.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r3.speaker: ابن جرير
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r3.claim: Ibn Jarir names the baker Majlatha and the cupbearer Nabwa.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r4.claim: After hearing the doomed prisoner's dream interpretation, he protested that they had only been playing.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r5.claim: The decree means either that the question and answer are finished or that its interpretation will soon be fulfilled.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r6.claim: Joseph's certainty about the interpretation may have come from revelation from God.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p38#2/r7.claim: Alternatively, as a prophet, Joseph could be certain of what God caused him to say, unlike a nonprophet.

QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r8.claim: The two prisoners shared a question and imprisonment but had opposite outcomes: one was executed and the other favored and elevated.

QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r9.claim: Dream interpretation, even when true, proceeds by predominance of probability rather than certainty.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r1.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r1.claim: The cupbearer's dream showed a vine with three branches and grapes that he pressed for the king; Joseph predicted his return to service after three days.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r2.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r2.claim: Joseph told the baker that his three baskets foretold execution by the king after three days, with birds eating from his head.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r3.claim: Joseph's firm prediction that the dreams would occur came from revelation; the fact that both men had fabricated their dreams yet the interpretations came true shows this.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, Qatāda, and others say “the matter is decided” only ends the requested interpretation, not a certain prediction.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r5.claim: Ibn Masʿūd agrees that يوسف's words finish the interpretation requested by the prisoners without guaranteeing its fulfillment.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r6.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r6.claim: Qatāda agrees that يوسف's words finish the interpretation requested by the prisoners without guaranteeing its fulfillment.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r7.claim: Al-Wāḥidī prefers the revelation-based certainty reading as more fitting to a prophet's state.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p120#2/r8.claim: The word الاستفتاء was explained earlier in the commentary on al-Nisāʾ.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:41-44/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:41-44/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:41-44/r1.claim: Joseph predicts that one companion will serve his master wine and the other will be crucified and eaten by birds; whether or not the dreams were genuine, the interpretation will happen.

JISHUMI:v5p3646/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3646/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3646/r5.claim: Qaḍā means completing and executing something fully; hence لما قضي means when it was finished, and a qāḍī is so named.

JISHUMI:v5p3646/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3646/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3646/r6.claim: Istiftāʾ is asking for a legal opinion; fatwā answers the legal question itself, not the reasoning behind it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r1.claim: The cupbearer will serve wine to his master, the king; after three days he will be released and restored to his former position.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r2.claim: The baker will be released after three days only to be crucified, so birds eat from his head.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p243#2/r3.claim: Ibn Masud says both men admitted they had invented the dreams and were only playing; Joseph answered that God’s decree was settled regardless.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r1.claim: The one who will serve wine is the cupbearer; one reading has him give his lord a drink, while ʿIkrima's reading uses a passive construction.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r2.speaker: عكرمة
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r2.claim: ʿIkrima reads yusqā rabbahu, with the passive meaning that he will be given drink to satisfy him.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r3.claim: Yusuf interprets the cupbearer's vine as the king and his good standing, with three days in prison before release; the baker's three baskets mean three days before execution.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r4.claim: Although the men asked about different dreams, al-amr means their shared accusation of poisoning and the outcome of their imprisonment: one would escape and one die.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p444#3/r5.claim: Alternatively, the men had fabricated the dreams to test Yusuf; he told them the outcome would occur whether they had spoken truthfully or lied.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r5.claim: Joseph reportedly told Banu he would return to his former position serving the king, and Majlath would be crucified, after three days.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r6.claim: One report says both prisoners denied having seen dreams and said they had invented them to test Joseph; another says only the man sentenced to crucifixion denied it, while a third says they saw them but later denied it.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r7.claim: Some read يسقي from saqā and others from asqā, two verbs with the same meaning; ʿIkrima and al-Jaḥdari read the passive form, meaning he will be given wine to drink.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r8.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p246/r8.claim: Joseph reports knowledge of the unseen granted by God and says the matter has already been decreed.

TABRISI:12:39-41/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:39-41/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:39-41/r8.claim: The cupbearer's three grape clusters meant three more days in prison, then release on the fourth day and restoration to his post; Yusuf calls his master 'lord' as one says lord of a house or estate.

TABRISI:12:39-41/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:39-41/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:39-41/r9.claim: The other prisoner's baskets meant three more days before he was crucified and birds ate from his head; Yusuf's certain forecast shows he spoke by revelation of the unseen, not ordinary interpretation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r1.speaker: ابن السائب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r1.claim: Ibn al-Sa'ib says rabb here means master; Joseph predicts that the cupbearer will serve wine to his master after three days and regain his old position.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r2.speaker: ابن السائب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r2.claim: Ibn al-Sa'ib says Joseph tells the baker that in three days the king will execute and crucify him, and birds will eat from his head.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r3.claim: “The matter is decided” means the interpretation has been settled, whether the prisoners' dreams were true or false.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r4.claim: One answer to why Joseph was certain is that revelation told him; the declaration that the matter was decided shows it was revealed.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p226#2/r5.claim: The alternative says he did not guarantee the events: “the matter is decided” may mean only that he has finished answering their question.

RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p107/r7.claim: Joseph could infer that they served the king from their use of rabb for their master in the later statements about serving wine and asking to be remembered.

RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r1.claim: Joseph interprets the cupbearer's vine as a return to service after three days, and the baker's three baskets as execution and birds eating from his head.

RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r2.claim: The two men later said they had seen nothing; one view is that they invented the dreams to test Joseph, while another says they disliked his answer.

RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says Joseph gave the interpretation rather than revelation; the verse's description of expectation as ظن also argues against certainty from revelation.

RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p114#2/r4.claim: He considers revelation possible: God may have disclosed each man's outcome when asked, though it appeared as dream interpretation; alternatively, Joseph's interpretive judgment need not mean an inevitable outcome.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r1.claim: Joseph told the cupbearer he would return to serving the king after three days, while the other man would be crucified after three days and eaten by birds; whether dreamed or not, the decree was settled.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r2.claim: Some linguists use سقى and أسقى synonymously; al-Nahhas says most distinguish giving someone water to drink from providing a source of water.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r3.claim: A false dream interpretation does not bind someone; Joseph's interpretation became a decree because he was a prophet and God made it occur to confirm his prophethood.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r4.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r4.claim: A report from Qatada says a man told Umar he dreamed of alternating lush growth and drought; Umar predicted alternating faith and apostasy ending in death as an unbeliever, and the man said he had dreamed nothing.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:41/r5.claim: The author says this sort of prediction was exceptional for Umar, a divinely inspired man whose intuitions and statements came true, citing two further examples.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:41/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:41/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:41/r1.claim: The cupbearer will return to serving his master wine, while the baker will be crucified and birds will eat from his head.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:41/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:41/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:41/r2.claim: The two men said Joseph had lied, and he replied that the matter they asked about was settled; it is singular because they sought to learn the shared outcome of their cases.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r1.claim: The cupbearer will return to serving his master wine and resume his former work; the baker will be crucified and birds will eat from his head.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r2.claim: Joseph interprets three vine branches as three days in prison, after which the cupbearer returns to his former station; three baskets mean the baker will be killed after three days.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p190/r3.claim: When the baker denied having seen anything after hearing the interpretation, Joseph said that the matter being asked about was settled: one would perish and the other escape.

QASHANI:12:41-42/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:41-42/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:41-42/r1.claim: The cupbearer's fate means that attachment to pleasures is imposed on the spirit after restraint from association.

QASHANI:12:41-42/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:41-42/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:41-42/r2.claim: The baker's crucifixion means suppressing desire and fixing it to vegetative nature so imagination and animal faculties cannot act through it; after desire dies, the soul's powers fulfill divine rights.

QASHANI:12:41-42/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:41-42/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:41-42/r3.claim: Their declared outcome marks Joseph's approach to God and the emergence of sainthood through annihilation in God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r10.speaker: عكرمة والجحدري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r10.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Jaḥdarī read the passive yusqā, meaning that the king will be given wine to drink.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r11.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r11.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya understands ربه as the prisoner's master.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r12.claim: Joseph tells the prisoners through knowledge from God that the outcome is decreed whether their dreams were genuine or feigned.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r13.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r13.claim: The singular الأمر refers to the final outcome of the accusation that jailed the men: one is saved and one killed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r4.claim: After delivering the more important teaching about religion, Joseph calls the men his prison companions again so they will focus on the interpretation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r5.claim: Joseph tells Bunū that he will return to his former post serving the king; three vine branches mean three more days in prison before release.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r6.claim: Joseph tells Malḥab that his three baskets mean three days until he is released and crucified.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r7.claim: Some reports say the men denied seeing anything because they had pretended to test Joseph; another says only the man told he would be crucified said this, while another says both saw and then denied it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r8.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r8.claim: The majority read yasqī from saqā; another group reads yusqī from asqā, and both verbs can mean the same thing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r9.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p278/r9.claim: The Lawāmiʿ author says saqā and asqā are synonyms, though the usual distinction is giving a drink versus providing water.

SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r1.speaker: العامة
SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r1.claim: The common reading فيسقي has an open yāʾ from سقاه يسقيه; عكرمة reads a damma from أسقى, a synonymous verb, also seen in the readings of 56:69.

SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r2.speaker: عكرمة والجحدري
SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r2.claim: They also read فيسقى ربه in the passive, with ربه nominative; al-Zamakhshari attributes this only to عكرمة.

SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:12:41/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari asks why قضي الأمر is singular when the two men asked about different outcomes, and answers that it means the matter for which they were accused and imprisoned.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r1.claim: Yusuf leaves the cupbearer's identity unstated to spare the other prisoner, though the first will serve his master and the other will be crucified and eaten by birds.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r2.claim: Yusuf says the matter is settled because a dream remains suspended until interpreted and then comes to pass.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r3.speaker: عبد الله
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r3.claim: Ibn Masud reports that the prisoners then denied having seen anything, prompting Yusuf to say their question was settled; Mujahid and others give the same explanation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r4.claim: Ibn Kathir generalizes that whoever invents a dream and receives an interpretation is bound by that interpretation.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r5.claim: Ahmad transmits from Muawiya ibn Hayda the Prophetic report that a dream is suspended until interpreted, after which it occurs.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p390/r6.claim: A report in Abu Ya'la's Musnad, through Anas, says a dream follows the first interpreter.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r1.claim: Calling them prison companions evokes shared hardship, which removes worldly pretension and softens the heart toward friendship.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r2.claim: Joseph leaves the identity of the condemned prisoner ambiguous, allowing each man to hope he is the one restored unless they demand a specific answer.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r3.claim: The cupbearer will serve wine to his master again; the baker will be crucified by the king and birds will eat from his head.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r4.claim: The passive verb for crucifixion reflects that only the king has authority to crucify; the paired clauses use ellipsis, with each outcome implying its opposite counterpart.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r5.claim: A report says the two men denied seeing anything and said they were playing, but Joseph insists their case is settled and his interpretation is neither ignorance nor error.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r6.speaker: الرماني
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r6.claim: Al-Rummani distinguishes fatwa as an answer about a matter's meaning from an answer that gives its underlying cause.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p43/r7.claim: The dreams may foreshadow the king's: pressed grapes signify green ears and fat cattle, while the birds eating the baker's bread signify dry ears and lean cattle.

DURR-FULL:v4p536/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p536/r1.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p536/r1.claim: Joseph predicted that Mujlab would be crucified and birds would eat from his head, while Nabwa would return to his post and regain his master's favor.

DURR-FULL:v4p538/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p538/r10.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v4p538/r10.claim: Ibn Masud says the prisoners invented the dreams to test Joseph; after he interpreted them they claimed to have been playing, but the interpretation had already fixed the outcome.

DURR-FULL:v4p538/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p538/r8.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v4p538/r8.claim: Ikrima describes the cupbearer's dream as planting a grape seed that grew clusters, pressing them, and serving the king; Joseph predicted three more prison days before his return to service.

DURR-FULL:v4p538/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p538/r9.speaker: ابن زيد
DURR-FULL:v4p538/r9.claim: Ibn Zayd says the cupbearer would serve his master, explaining rabbahu as his lord or master.

DURR-FULL:v4p540/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r1.speaker: أبو مجلز
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r1.claim: Abu Majliz says one of the two prisoners who described a dream to Joseph was lying.

DURR-FULL:v4p540/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r2.claim: Mujahid says the decision was fixed when the prisoners claimed they had made up the dreams: their real dreams had taken effect as Joseph interpreted them.

DURR-FULL:v4p540/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r3.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r3.claim: Qatadah identifies the doomed man as the baker and the restored man as the cupbearer; both denied having dreamed, but Joseph's prediction stood.

DURR-FULL:v4p540/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r4.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v4p540/r4.claim: Ikrima recited the clause with the wording أما أحدكما فيسقي ربه خمرا.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r1.claim: After proving his knowledge, Joseph resumes the answer with a repeated address because interpretation is a new topic; he means the cupbearer without naming him, trusting the interpretation and observing good companionship.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r2.claim: Joseph interprets the cupbearer’s vine as the king and restored favor; three branches mean three days until release and return to service. The baker’s three baskets mean three days until release and crucifixion, with birds eating his head.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r3.claim: A reading has yusqā passive; another uses active asqā. Saqā and asqā can both mean giving drink, though convention distinguishes giving a drink from providing watering; ʿIkrima is also reported to read passively with riyyihi as second object.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p245#2/r4.claim: Quḍiya means completed or settled: the matter the two men asked about has been decided.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r1.claim: The prisoners' visions foreshadow one man's rescue and the other's destruction; their questioning asks for the visions' interpretation.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r10.claim: The report of Joseph's answer may be a rebuttal to the prisoners' denial or a confirmation of his interpretation; a lie by the cupbearer could have protected his companion, and another report says the baker was the one who denied it.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r11.claim: The episode is cited for the maxim that dreams occur as first interpreted, expressed in the saying that a dream rests on a bird's wing until told, then falls.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r2.speaker: ابن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r2.claim: Ibn Masud reports that the two prisoners feigned dreams to test Joseph; after he interpreted them, they said they had been playing and had seen nothing.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r3.speaker: بعض المحققين
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r3.claim: An unnamed investigator says the settled matter is the dreams themselves, not the men's eventual fates, because an inquiry seeks an answer about an incident, not its outcome.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r4.claim: The investigator argues that asking for interpretation means asking about the dreams as events, analogizing the king's request to be advised about his dream.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r5.speaker: بعض المحققين
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r5.claim: He reads the wording as magnifying the dreams: the text calls them an affair and their request an inquiry because such inquiry concerns obscure, momentous cases; the present tense prolongs the request until Joseph finishes answering.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r6.speaker: بعض المحققين
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r6.claim: He explains the singular 'matter' despite two dreams as matching the prisoners' own singular wording, and says they asked about the image of the outcome rather than their crime or its cause.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r7.claim: Al-Alusi objects that the investigator's distinction between the matter and the event is inconsistent: if the outcome and dream are treated as identical for predication, they can also be identical for inquiry.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r8.speaker: الكثير
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r8.claim: Many exegetes take the matter as the men's eventual outcome and understand the preposition causally: they asked about the dreams in order to learn their fate; Al-Alusi finds this the stronger, less strained reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r9.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v12p246/r9.claim: Another view takes the matter as the crime for which the men were accused and imprisoned, supplying an omitted noun meaning the consequence of that accusation.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r1.claim: Joseph's vocative stresses the importance of his interpretation and addresses them as fellow prisoners.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r2.claim: If Joseph spoke in the order shown, he gave both interpretations together in a veiled summary so the condemned man could work out his fate gradually.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r3.claim: Alternatively, the verse may condense Joseph's original speech, in which he directly assigned each interpretation to one man.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r4.claim: “The matter is decided” confirms the interpretation because their urgent question concerned what would happen to them in prison.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p277/r5.claim: Istiftāʾ is asking for a fatwa: an explanation that resolves difficulty or uncertainty; the verb aftā retains its hamza and is linked by some to fatā, youth, because clear explanation strengthens the recipient.

TABATABAI:12:40-41#2/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:40-41#2/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:40-41#2/r6.claim: The two predictions in this verse interpret the two prisoners’ dreams respectively: the cupbearer’s dream of pressing wine and the other prisoner’s dream of birds eating from his head.

TABATABAI:12:41-42#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:41-42#2/r2.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:12:41-42#2/r2.claim: The same report identifies the two young men as the king’s servants, a baker and a cupbearer, and says the baker had fabricated the dream and was the one crucified.

TABATABAI:12:41-42/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:41-42/r1.speaker: أئمة أهل البيت عليهم السلام
TABATABAI:12:41-42/r1.claim: An Imami report says the second prisoner admitted that he had invented his dream after hearing that he would be crucified; Joseph replied that the matter he had asked about was already decreed.

TABATABAI:12:41-42/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:41-42/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:41-42/r4.claim: The view that Joseph interpreted the dreams only by conjecture conflicts with his declaration that the matter was settled and God’s statement that He taught him interpretation.

ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.claim: Unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may hate what is good for them or love what is bad for them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Prophets seize opportunities to invite people to God's message; Joseph preached monotheism before interpreting the prisoners' dreams.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:39/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:39/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:39/r1.claim: Ibn Ashur reports that Egyptians of the time had about thirty gods representing natural forces or stars.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:39/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:39/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:39/r3.claim: Joseph interprets one prisoner’s dream as his return to serving his master and serving wine, and the other’s as crucifixion with birds pecking his head.

STUDYQURAN:12:41/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:41/r1.speaker: N and Kl
STUDYQURAN:12:41/r1.claim: The wine carrier would survive and regain his former post serving wine to Egypt’s king.

STUDYQURAN:12:41/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:41/r2.speaker: My
STUDYQURAN:12:41/r2.claim: The baker would be crucified for his crime, and birds would eat from his head after death.
